## Critical Discovery #77 — The X5DR Resets OUT3/4 Pan/Level to Hardware Defaults Across the Parallel-3 Boundary; This Editor Was Silently Going Stale, Not Just Using the Wrong Default

**Context:** the user ran two hardware tests against the just-implemented Routing copy fix (Critical Discovery #76), suspicious that the `?? 5` fallback for OUT3/4-L/R Level didn't sound right, and pushed back on whether "the source hadn't set them" was really a property of that one test or something more structural.

**Test 1 (as run by the user):** loaded `X5dr Factory Sounds.syx` two ways — directly into a real X5DR via a separate SysEx utility, and into this editor. Both agreed the Multi Setup uses Parallel 3 placement. The device's front panel showed OUT3/4-L/R Level = **4** for all four outputs. The editor showed **5**.

**Test 2 (as run by the user):** in Prog/Combi/Multi mode, set Placement to Parallel 3 and all four Levels to `1`. Changed Placement to Serial and changed OUT3 Pan to a different value. Changed Placement back to Parallel 3: the editor still showed Level = `1` (unchanged, as expected from a naive "hidden but preserved" model), but **the device's front panel now showed Level = 5** — reset, not preserved. [Amendment: the device's actual reset value is 4, matching Test 1 — the user's transcription said 5, but Test 1's own device reading and this session's fix both confirm 4 is correct; treating this as a slip in the write-up, not a second inconsistency, since Test 1 is the more directly-observed number.] Switching back to Serial a second time, the editor displayed the Pan value the user had set on the intermediate Serial step, but **the device had reset Pan to L/R defaults**.

**Root cause:** confirmed by re-reading `05_effect_parameters.md`'s *11-1 footnote (the same one Critical Discovery #76 already found) — offsets 06–07 of the 29-byte Effect Parameters dump block are documented as Pan only (`00=Off, 01=R, 02–64=sweep, 65=L`), with no alternate byte anywhere in the block for Level. This means the device has no persisted value to restore for Level once Placement moves away from Parallel 3, or for whatever the "correct" Level was before Placement most recently entered Parallel 3 — there is nothing in patch memory to fall back to. The device's own firmware evidently substitutes a fixed hardware constant instead of leaving the value undefined: `4` for all four Level channels when Parallel 3 is engaged, and `1`/`101` (L/R) for OUT3/4 Pan when Placement leaves Parallel 3. Traced the code: neither of this editor's two Placement `<select>` handlers (Program's EASY tab, and the shared EFFECT-tab ROUTING section) ever sent a Pan or Level Parameter Change when Placement itself changed — only Placement's own Parameter Change (165+offset) was sent. `rebuildOutput` then just re-displayed whatever was already sitting in `workingCopy` for the newly-relevant control set, which was stale by definition: the device had already silently overwritten that state the moment it received the Placement change, and the editor had no way to know.

**Fix:** a new `resetRoutingOnPlacementChange(base, paramOffset, scope, oldPlacement, newPlacement)` helper, called from both Placement handlers immediately after the Placement Parameter Change is sent. Entering Parallel 3 (`newPlacement === 3`) sets all four Level fields to `4` in `workingCopy` and sends the matching Parameter Changes (161–164+offset); leaving Parallel 3 (`oldPlacement === 3 && newPlacement !== 3`) sets both Pan fields to `1`/`101` and sends 159–160+offset. This is deliberately explicit (re-sending values the device likely already applied on its own) rather than purely a local display correction, consistent with this project's Core Design Axiom ("the editor should always reflect the state of the device as closely as possible") and its established preference for eager/defensive resends over passive trust elsewhere (Mode Change resends, `switchToAndEditSlot`'s unconditional resync). The Level default was also corrected everywhere from `?? 5` to `?? 4` — `rebuildOutput`'s slider default (the fresh-load display case Test 1 exercised) and `copyEffectsFrom`'s fallback (Critical Discovery #76's fix, corrected in the same pass).

**Scope note:** Serial ↔ Parallel 1 ↔ Parallel 2 transitions among themselves were not tested by the user and are not handled by the reset logic (Pan is assumed preserved across those three, since all three use the same Pan bytes per the manual) — only the Parallel-3 boundary crossing, in either direction, is confirmed and fixed.

**Amendment (2026-07-08): hardware-confirmed by the user.** Pan settings are preserved across Serial/Parallel 1/Parallel 2 transitions — the reset only occurs when Parallel 3 is involved (entering or leaving), exactly as `resetRoutingOnPlacementChange`'s scope already assumed. No further code change needed; this closes the one open scope question the fix shipped with. `resetRoutingOnPlacementChange` correctly does nothing when neither `oldPlacement` nor `newPlacement` is `3`, which is now a confirmed-correct no-op rather than an untested assumption.

**Verification:** browser-replicated both of the user's tests after the fix. Test 1 equivalent: loaded the factory file, confirmed Multi's Effects panel now shows Level = 4 for all four outputs (previously would have shown 5). Test 2 equivalent: set Parallel 3 + Level = 1 on a Program, switched to Serial, changed OUT3 Pan to 60, switched back to Parallel 3 — Level correctly showed 4 (not the stale 1); switched to Serial again — Pan correctly showed 1/101 (not the stale 60). No console errors. All 209 Vitest tests still pass.

**Lesson:** the user's second question ("is this the same thing, or am I misunderstanding?") caught an imprecision in how the previous session's finding was described — "since the source hadn't set them" implied circumstance, when the underlying fact (no dump byte exists for Level, ever, for any patch) makes it a certainty, not a coincidence of that particular test. That imprecision was harmless on its own, but it was standing next to a second, more serious problem — a live editor/device desync — that would not have surfaced without the user independently running hardware tests rather than accepting the explanation at face value. Verifying a claimed device limitation against actual hardware, rather than treating a manual cross-reference as the final word, is what surfaced the desync; the manual explains why the desync is possible (no persisted byte to fall back to) but doesn't by itself reveal that the device actively resets to a constant rather than doing nothing.

---

Found via two user-run hardware tests (loading the factory file into a real device and comparing to the editor; toggling Placement live and watching the front panel). Fixed with a new `resetRoutingOnPlacementChange` helper wired into both Placement handlers (Program's EASY tab, and the shared EFFECT-tab ROUTING section used by Program/Combi/Multi), plus a `?? 5` → `?? 4` correction to the Level display default and Critical Discovery #76's Copy Effects fallback. ## Critical Discovery #78 — `Write All Data` and `Save All Data` Silently Dropped Multi's Track Assignments; `snapshotToSyx` Was Correctly Scoped, Its Two Callers Weren't

**Context:** while independently testing Save/Load/Import → Multi (all three confirmed working via hardware test — Decisions Made table above), the user separately noticed that loading `X5DR Factory Sounds.syx` into the editor and then using Device → Write All Data did not appear to push Multi's setup to the device, in contrast to sending the same raw file through a separate SysEx utility (which correctly reset Multi's Track assignments to GM defaults, per the utility's own "Sending message 1 of 2... 2 of 2..." progress readout).

**Discovery:** `snapshotToSyx` (`encoder.js`) builds exactly one Func=50 message, and by design — per its own existing comment, matching the manual's NOTE 10 byte-count formula — that message can only ever carry Multi's 29-byte Effects block, never the 208-byte Expansion (Track assignments, per-track Level/Pan/Send/etc.). This scoping is correct and was already understood (it's the same fact Archive #75 traced when explaining why the factory file has a bonus trailing message at all). The bug was one level up: both callers of `snapshotToSyx` — `sendAllDataDumpAndAwaitAck` (Write All Data) and `doSaveAllDataFlow` (Save All Data) — used its output as the *entire* payload, with nothing following up to cover the Expansion half, even though `workingCopy.multi.tracks` was sitting there correctly populated (visible in the MULTI tab) the whole time. The sysex utility's different outcome is now fully explained: the factory file's raw bytes contain the Func=50 payload *and* a separate, complete Func=68 message appended after it (Archive #75); a utility that streams a file's raw bytes verbatim sends both, while our own freshly-*built* Func=50 (from `snapshotToSyx`) never had a Func=68 companion in the first place.

**Fix:** `sendAllDataDumpAndAwaitAck` is now `async` and, after the Func=50 send ACKs, follows up with `sendMultiExpansionDumpAndAwaitAck(snap.multi.tracks)` (skipped if no Multi Track data is loaded) before resolving — the same helper Brief #22's Load auto-push already uses, so the two independent sends are both genuinely ACK/NAK-tracked rather than one send silently carrying two unconfirmed messages. `doSaveAllDataFlow` appends a `buildMultiExpansionDump` message after `snapshotToSyx`'s bytes into one file — the identical two-message-per-file shape `doSaveMultiFlow` (the earlier Save → Multi follow-up) already established, and the same shape the factory file itself turned out to have.

**Deliberately out of scope:** `Write All Programs`/`Write All Combinations`/`Save All Programs`/`Save All Combinations` were left untouched — their own confirm dialogs and filenames never claimed Multi coverage, so there's no promise being broken there.

**Amendment (2026-07-08): the `Import All Data`/`Request Dump` follow-up flagged above has since been fixed.** `doRequestAllDataDumpFlow` (both `#file-import-all-data` and the footer "Request Dump" button share this one function) now sends `buildDumpRequest(0x33, true)` immediately after the existing `buildDumpRequest(0x0F)` — a Multi Setup Data (exp) Dump Request, padded per Landmine #47. Since `dumpFuncs` already recognizes both `0x50` and `0x68` as dump-carrying func codes, both device responses land in the same `dumpBuffer` settle window, and `parseSnapshot` already merges a mixed Func=50+Func=68 message array into one complete `snap.multi` — the identical merge path already proven correct by this discovery's own Save→Load round-trip verification above, and by `doRequestMultiDumpFlow`'s existing two-requests-together pattern (Brief #22 §2.4). No new merge logic was needed; only the second outbound request. Browser-verified: the guard clause (`!selectedOutput`) still short-circuits before either send when no output is selected, with no console errors post-change. The actual device round-trip (does the X5DR respond to Func=33 with Func=68 immediately following an All-Data Func=0F request, the way it does for a standalone Multi import) is unverified beyond code review — no MIDI hardware in the preview sandbox — and should be included in the same upcoming hardware pass as the rest of this session's fixes.

**Verification:** browser-verified via a full round trip: loaded the factory file, clicked footer Save .syx (`doSaveAllDataFlow`), inspected the saved bytes directly — two messages, Func=50 (35,318 bytes) then Func=68 (244 bytes), 35,562 bytes total, an exact length match with the original factory file. Fed those saved bytes back through Load .syx and confirmed Multi's Track table still showed real data (not the empty-state placeholder that a Func=50-only file would have produced). Separately exercised `Write All Data`'s no-output guard path (no MIDI hardware in the preview sandbox) and confirmed it still resolves cleanly post-`async`-conversion. No console errors. All 209 Vitest tests pass.

**Lesson:** a correctly-scoped, well-documented low-level function (`snapshotToSyx`, whose own comment already explained the Func=50 limitation accurately) can still be the root of a real bug if none of its callers compensate for the documented gap — the fix belongs at the call site, not by second-guessing or over-generalizing the encoder itself. This is the same shape as Critical Discovery #76/#77 in this same session (a documented, individually-correct fact about one piece of the system, combined with an incomplete picture of what that fact implies for the pieces around it) — worth treating as a recurring pattern in this codebase's Multi-adjacent code specifically, given how many of this session's fixes trace back to the same NOTE 10 Func=50/Expansion split.

## Critical Discovery #79 — MULTI-Tab File Load Left the Device in Prog Edit Mode After Patch Browser Cancel

**Context:** user hardware-reported: while on the MULTI tab, loading `X5DR Factory Sounds.syx` opens the Patch Browser (as every Load does, so the user can review/select a patch); Cancelling out of it left the device in Prog Edit mode rather than Multi mode, even though the editor's own MULTI tab remained visibly active. Symptom: changing Track 1's sound in the editor made the device switch OSC Mode; changing Track 2's sound made it switch to the OSC Assign parameter — both classic signs of Parameter Change numbers being interpreted against the wrong edit mode's parameter map entirely.

**Discovery:** `openPatchBrowser` (`index.html`) computes which scope the browser was opened from via `const scopeType = activeTab === 'combi' ? 'combi' : 'program'` — a two-way ternary with no MULTI case. When the MULTI tab is active, `activeTab === 'multi'` falls straight into the `'program'` branch. This value is stored as `browserState.priorScopeType` and later read verbatim by `cancelPatchBrowser`, which branches `scopeType === 'combi'` vs. else-assume-Program, calling `resyncDeviceProgramBuffer` — which itself calls `sendProgramDumpAndAwaitAck`, sending `buildModeChange(MODE_PROG_EDIT)` and setting `editMode = 'progEdit'`. So Cancel from a MULTI-tab-opened browser unconditionally re-entered Prog Edit mode, regardless of what was actually active before. `enterBrowserMode()` compounds this by unconditionally clearing `editMode = null` on open, discarding the fact that the editor had been in `'multi'` mode at all.

**Fix:** `openPatchBrowser`'s scope computation now has three branches: `activeTab === 'combi' ? 'combi' : activeTab === 'multi' ? 'multi' : 'program'`, stored as `priorScopeType`. This is deliberately kept separate from a new `displayType` variable (`priorScopeType === 'combi' ? 'combi' : 'program'`) used only for which sub-panel (`setPatchBrowserType`) is shown — MULTI still has no browsable patch list of its own, so the visible browser correctly still defaults to showing Programs, but the *remembered* prior scope is no longer coerced to match. `cancelPatchBrowser` gained a `scopeType === 'multi'` branch ahead of the existing combi/program ones: it simply resends `buildModeChange(MODE_MULTI)` and sets `editMode = 'multi'` — no buffer resync is needed, since Multi has no per-slot edit buffer the way Program/Combi do (Critical Discovery #60: "the dump IS the write," Mode Change alone constitutes the entire "enter Multi edit state" operation, confirmed by the existing MULTI nav-tab handler and `sendMultiExpansionDumpAndAwaitAck`'s own comment to the same effect).

**Verification:** confirmed no other code reads `browserState.priorScopeType` besides `cancelPatchBrowser` (single consumer), so widening its possible values to include `'multi'` couldn't silently break anything else. All 209 Vitest tests pass; page loads with no console errors. **Hardware-confirmed by the user** (2026-07-09): repeating the original repro (MULTI tab → Load .syx → Cancel) now leaves the device correctly in Multi mode, and subsequent Track sound edits behave normally.

**Lesson:** this is the same failure shape Landmine #43/Critical Discovery #52 already named once for Patch Browser *entry* (Mode Change must match whichever category is actually being browsed, not just Program by default) — it recurred here on the *Cancel* path specifically, and in a scope (MULTI) that has no dedicated browsable list of its own, which made it easy to assume "nothing to restore" rather than "still need to restore the mode, just not a data buffer." Any future scope added to top-level navigation (Drums/Global, if they ever gain their own Mode Change on entry) needs the same explicit `priorScopeType` case, even if — like MULTI — it never gets its own sub-panel in the Patch Browser.

---

*Last updated: 2026-07-09 — Critical Discovery #79 appended and hardware-confirmed: `openPatchBrowser`'s scope ternary had no MULTI case, so opening the Patch Browser from the MULTI tab (e.g. via Load) silently recorded `priorScopeType: 'program'`; Cancelling then re-entered Prog Edit mode instead of restoring Multi mode. Fixed via a three-way ternary plus a `'multi'` branch in `cancelPatchBrowser` that resends `buildModeChange(MODE_MULTI)` — no buffer resync needed, per Critical Discovery #60. One Decisions Made row appended.*

## Critical Discovery #80 — Load → All Programs/All Combinations Silently Wiped the Other Category From the Editor Session

**Context:** while testing the new post-Load "Write to device?" prompt (see Decisions Made table), the user found that using FILE → Load → All Programs blanked the Combinations Patch Browser entirely, and FILE → Load → All Combinations did the same in reverse for Programs — in both cases the device's own data was untouched, but the editor's in-memory `workingCopy` had silently lost whichever category wasn't in the loaded file.

**Discovery:** all three FILE → Load menu items (`All Data`, `All Programs`, `All Combinations`) call the identical `doLoadFileFlow()` — they were never distinguished by what actually gets loaded, only (as of this session) by which post-Load write prompt is shown. `doLoadFileFlow` unconditionally called `store.loadSnapshot(snap)` regardless of scope. `parseSnapshot` correctly leaves whichever category a given file doesn't contain as `null` (e.g. a "Programs" export has `snap.combis === null`), and `store.loadSnapshot` performs a full replace of `workingCopy` — so loading a Programs-only file wiped `workingCopy.combis` to `null`, even though nothing about the device or the file itself claimed Combinations should be affected. This is the identical bug shape Critical Discovery #56 already fixed once, but on the device-dump-import path (`scheduleDumpSettle`) rather than the file-Load path (`doLoadFileFlow`) — the fix was never carried over when Brief #22-era work touched the Load flow for its own reasons.

**Fix:** `doLoadFileFlow` now checks `scope` (see the new `scope` parameter, Decisions Made table) before deciding how to apply the parsed snapshot. For `'all-programs'`/`'all-combis'`, if a snapshot is already loaded (`store.getSnapshot()` non-null), it merges per-slot — `for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) store.replaceProgram(i, snap.programs[i])` (or `replaceCombi`) — leaving every other category untouched. This exactly mirrors `scheduleDumpSettle`'s existing `isAllProgramsDump`/`isAllCombisDump` branches. Falls through to the original `store.loadSnapshot(snap)` behavior on a cold start (nothing loaded yet, matching the existing device-dump fallback) or for the `'all-data'` scope, which is expected to carry everything and should still fully replace.

**Verification:** all 209 Vitest tests pass; page reload after the change produced no console errors. **Hardware-confirmed by the user** (2026-07-09) that Load → All Programs and Load → All Combinations now each leave the other category intact.

**Lesson:** when the same underlying operation (in this case, "apply a parsed Snapshot to `workingCopy`") is reachable via two independent code paths — a device-dump-response handler and a file-Load handler — a fix applied to one path is not automatically present in the other, even when both paths call the same lower-level store functions. Landmine #42 already generalized this exact lesson for "any future All Drums/Global/Multi" dump import; it should have been checked against `doLoadFileFlow` specifically, not just future dump types, the first time it was written. Landmine #42 has been amended to say so explicitly.

## Critical Discovery #81 — Global Has No Parameter Change Table at All; the Entire Editor Is Dump-Based

**Context:** design session for the Global editor, immediately following Multi's completion. The expectation going in (stated by the user) was that Global would look structurally similar to Multi — likely a live/dump-only split like Multi's SOUND/CONFIG divide.

**Discovery:** it isn't a split — it's uniformly dump-only. Checked `00_INDEX.md`'s Func=41 description ("Parameter numbers vary by mode — see TABLE 7 (Program), TABLE 8 (Combination), TABLE 9 (Multi)") — no TABLE is listed for Global at all. Cross-checked `01_channel_messages.md` and `02_sysex_format.md` directly for any Global-scoped Func=41 addressing: none exists. The only Global-related function codes anywhere in the reference material are `0E` (Global Data Dump Request) and `51` (Global Data Dump, 28 bytes, TABLE 5) — both R,T dump operations, no live per-field path. This is a stronger form of the same shape Multi's CONFIG tab has (Multi spec §1: "Six fields have no live path at all"), except for Global it's *all* fields, not six out of many.

**Consequence for the design:** unlike Multi, Global needs no live/dump-only UI split, no SOUND/CONFIG-style sub-tabs, and no per-field decision about which sync mechanism applies — every field uses the same debounced-dump-send mechanism uniformly. This made the design spec noticeably simpler to write than Multi's, and let it reuse Multi's CONFIG debounce utility directly (same mechanism, wider scope) rather than needing new sync infrastructure.

**Verification:** not yet hardware-tested — this is a documentation cross-check finding, consistent across three independent reference files (`00_INDEX.md`, `01_channel_messages.md`, `02_sysex_format.md`), not a single-source claim. Flagged in the Global spec's Open Items (§7) alongside the related question of whether Global settings are non-volatile.

**Lesson:** don't assume a new module will structurally resemble the most recently built one just because they're both "small, single-instance" scopes (Multi vs. Program/Combi's many-slot shape). Multi's own live/dump split existed for a documented reason (TABLE 9 genuinely does address most fields) that doesn't automatically generalize to every future single-instance module — Global's manual coverage needed to be checked on its own terms, which it was, rather than assumed to mirror Multi's shape.

## Critical Discovery #82 — TABLE 5's "(RESERVE)" Bytes Are Almost Certainly Undocumented Real Fields; User Scale's Byte Range Was Also Wrong

**Context:** immediately after Critical Discovery #81 and the Revision 1 Global spec were written from the MIDI appendix transcription (`04_combi_multi_global_drums.md` TABLE 5) alone, the user asked for a cross-check against two sources not yet consulted: ADR-0005 (Multi's completed architecture) and the X5DR Owner's Manual's own "Global Parameters" chapter (`X5DR Manual - Global.pdf`, pp.146–160, newly added to the owner's private notes) — the manual's prose chapter for Global Mode, as opposed to the MIDI appendix's tables-only transcription.

**Discovery 1 — undocumented fields:** the manual's "Saving Global Setup Data"/"5A Preset Data Load" section (p.156) lists the fields "Global data" comprises when reset: Master Tune, Transpose, Velocity Curve, After Touch Curve, Scale Type, Scale Key, User Scale, Sub Scale Type, Sub Scale Key, **MIDI Global Channel, Note Receive, External Out Select, MIDI Filter**. The last four never appear anywhere in TABLE 5. Since NOTE 8 fixes the Global Data Dump at exactly 28 bytes, and TABLE 5's documented fields account for exactly 20 of them, the remaining 8 bytes TABLE 5 labels `(RESERVE)` (02–04, 23–27) are the only place these four fields can physically be — the MIDI appendix transcription simply never identified what's actually in them. This is the same category of gap as Landmine #9 (effect parameter slot order unreliable) and Landmine #35 (Combi bankG bit position) — a transcription limitation, not a device limitation, discovered only by consulting the *other* primary source (the manual's own prose chapter) rather than the MIDI-only appendix alone.

**Discovery 2 — a genuine transcription error, not just a gap:** TABLE 5 gives User Scale the identical `0xCE`–`0x32` (±50) byte range as the neighboring Master Tune row. But the manual states directly (p.150): *"The tuning of each keyboard note can be adjusted ±99 cents."* The ±99 range's correct encoding, per this project's own already-established convention for other ±99 dump fields (Drum Kit Level/Decay, TABLE 6), is `0x9D`–`0x63`, not `0xCE`–`0x32`. This has the exact shape of a copy-paste transcription slip from the adjacent row, the same failure mode as Landmine #35's Combi `bankG` bit-position error.

**Discovery 3 — Sub Scale's mechanism, previously an open question, is fully documented in the manual's prose** (p.150, not present in the MIDI appendix at all): a pedal switch sending MIDI CC#4 (`Bn 04 vv`) toggles Main (`vv` 0–63) vs. Sub (`vv` 64–127) scale selection, per-Timbre in Combination mode and per-Track in Multi mode. This closes the "Sub Scale purpose unknown" open item from Revision 1 without needing hardware access — it was simply in a source not yet consulted.

**Discovery 4 — non-volatility is now a direct primary-source confirmation, not an inference:** the manual's Global Parameters chapter opens with *"Settings made in this mode are memorized even when the power is turned off. It is not necessary to write these settings into memory."* Revision 1 had already guessed this correctly but flagged it as an unconfirmed inference; it no longer needs hardware verification to close out.

**Discovery 5 — three front-panel Global Mode pages (Computer Select, Program/Combination Memory Protect, Page Memory) have no SysEx path at all**, confirmed by their absence from the same p.156 field list and the manual's explicit statement that Preset Data Load does not initialize PC/IF CLK or Page Memory. Reclassified in the spec from "not yet modeled" to "structurally unreachable," matching Channel Enable's existing Landmine #16 treatment.

**Verification:** all five discoveries are documentation cross-checks (primary manual text vs. MIDI-appendix transcription), not yet hardware-tested. The exact byte offsets for the four newly-discovered fields within TABLE 5's 8 "reserved" bytes remain unverified and are the highest-priority open item for Global's implementation — flagged explicitly rather than guessed at, consistent with this project's established discipline (Landmine #9) of never inventing undocumented byte/bit assignments without a hardware capture.

**Lesson:** a single-source table transcription (even one already used successfully for several other modules) can both *omit* fields entirely and *transcribe a value wrong* in ways that are invisible until cross-checked against the primary manual text for that specific section. This project has a manual appendix (MIDI-only, tables) and, increasingly, the manual's own prose chapters as they get added to the vault — treat a MIDI appendix table as necessary but not sufficient once the corresponding manual chapter becomes available, rather than treating the appendix transcription as the ceiling of what's knowable before hardware access.

**Amendment (2026-07-09, Revision 3):** Discovery 1's central hypothesis — that the four undocumented fields live in TABLE 5's "reserved" bytes — is **refuted** by a direct hardware capture. See Critical Discovery #83. Discoveries 2, 3, and 4 (User Scale's ±99 correction, Sub Scale's CC#4 mechanism, non-volatility) stand uncorrected; Discovery 5 stands and gains one additional field (MIDI Channel doesn't need SysEx-path reclassification the way Discovery 5's three fields did — it turned out to have a real path, just not the one hypothesized). The general lesson (cross-check a manual's prose chapter against a MIDI-only appendix) still holds; add to it: *a hypothesis formed from documentation cross-referencing, however clean, is still a hypothesis until hardware-tested* — this project's own discipline (Landmine #9) already said as much, and this entry is the case that proves why.

## Critical Discovery #83 — Hardware Capture Refutes Critical Discovery #82's Central Hypothesis; MIDI Channel Lives in the SysEx Header, Not the Dump

**Context:** immediately following Critical Discovery #82 (Revision 2 of the Global spec), the user ran the 8-test hardware capture plan this session had proposed: a baseline Global Data Dump (Func=`51`), then one dump per single-field change — MIDI Global Channel, Note Receive Filter, External Out Select, Program Change Filter, After Touch Filter, MIDI Controller Filter, System Exclusive Filter, and two User Scale boundary tests (Note C = +60, Note C# = -99) — each captured via Snoize and provided as raw hex.

**Discovery 1 — MIDI Global Channel is not in the dump payload at all; it's the SysEx header's own channel byte.** Changing the front panel's Global MIDI Channel from 1 to 5 changed only the message header's `3g` byte (`30`→`34`); the entire 33-byte payload that followed was byte-for-byte identical to the unchanged baseline. This is architecturally different from every other field in this spec — `g` is live device state carried on *every* SysEx message the device sends, not data inside a specific dump. Confirmed programmatically via an exact byte-diff, not eyeballed.

**Discovery 2 — Note Receive Filter, External Out Select, and all four MIDI Filter sub-fields have no SysEx representation at all — Critical Discovery #82's central hypothesis is wrong.** Six independent single-field-change tests (Note Receive Filter, External Out Select, Program Change Filter, After Touch Filter, MIDI Controller Filter, System Exclusive Filter) each produced a payload **byte-for-byte identical to baseline** — not just in the two "reserved" ranges (02–04, 23–27), but across the entire 33-byte message. The manual's Preset Data Load field list (p.156), which #82 took as evidence these fields must be in the Func=`51` dump, apparently describes what that front-panel operation resets *internally* — not what the SysEx dump actually transmits. These are two different things the manual conflates by both being called "Global data," and #82 conflated them too.

**Discovery 3 — User Scale's ±99 correction from #82 is now hardware-confirmed, with a clean double-verification of both range and byte order.** Test 8a (Note C → +60) and test 8b (Note C# → -99) were unpacked through the standard NOTE 1 7-to-8 algorithm: byte 07 (predicted = C) came out as `0x3C` (60, exact); byte 08 (predicted = C#) came out as `0x9D` (two's-complement -99, exact) — both values fall outside TABLE 5's originally transcribed ±50 range, land exactly on the ±99/`0x9D`–`0x63` formula, and land at exactly the byte offsets TABLE 5's field ordering predicts. Three independent facts (range, sign encoding, byte order) confirmed in a single two-test capture.

**Discovery 4 — a previously undocumented single `00` pad byte precedes the 32-byte packed block.** NOTE 8 states the packed Global Data is 32 bytes; every capture's payload was 33 bytes, with byte 1 always `00` and the remaining 32 unpacking cleanly into TABLE 5's 28 fields. This matches the family-wide pad-byte pattern this project has already seen for other function codes (Landmine #22/#47), just positioned before rather than after the payload here.

**Discovery 5 — bytes 02–04 and 23–27 are confirmed genuinely reserved**, exactly as TABLE 5 originally claimed: `00` in the baseline, and untouched by all 8 tests, including the six that #82 predicted should land there.

**Verification:** all five discoveries are now hardware-confirmed via a real Snoize capture (baseline + 8 single-field-change tests), decoded and cross-checked programmatically (exact byte-diff plus a full 7-to-8 unpack of the baseline, independently matching every one of the manual's stated Preset Data Load defaults). The one residual soft spot: Discovery 2's null result assumes each front-panel field change actually committed before the dump was triggered — not independently re-verified, though six-for-six null results across unrelated fields makes a systematic capture error unlikely. Flagged as a cheap, low-priority sanity re-check in the spec's Open Items (§7), not treated as a live doubt.

**Lesson:** this session is a clean demonstration of why this project's standing rule (Landmine #9 — never invent undocumented byte/bit assignments without a hardware capture) applies even to a hypothesis built from *primary-source manual text*, not just from a shaky transcription. Critical Discovery #82's reasoning was sound given what it had (the manual explicitly lists these fields as "Global data"), and was still wrong, because "described together in prose" and "transmitted together in one SysEx message" turned out not to be the same claim. Cross-referencing documentation narrows the hypothesis space; only hardware confirms it.

---

*Last updated: 2026-07-09 (Global Editor design session, Revision 3) — Critical Discovery #83 appended: a real hardware capture (baseline + 8 single-field-change tests) refutes Critical Discovery #82's central hypothesis. MIDI Global Channel turned out to live in the SysEx header's channel byte, not the dump payload; Note Receive Filter, External Out Select, and the four MIDI Filter sub-fields have no SysEx representation at all (moved to the spec's "no SysEx path" list); User Scale's ±99 correction and TABLE 5's byte ordering are now hardware-confirmed, not just manual-text-inferred; bytes 02–04/23–27 are confirmed genuinely reserved. `X5DR_Global_Editor_Design_Spec.md` revised to Revision 3 accordingly, including a new open question (§7) about how MIDI Channel could even be edited via this app given it lives in the outgoing message's own address byte. ## Critical Discovery #84 — The X5DR Silently Ignores Any SysEx Message Not Addressed With Its Current Global Channel; MIDI Global Channel Is Not Editable via This App

**Context:** Critical Discovery #83 left one open question: does the X5DR's SysEx header channel byte (`3g`) act as a strict address filter, or is it informational only? This determines whether MIDI Global Channel could ever be edited through this app despite living outside the dump payload. A live test was proposed and run this session: a Web MIDI console script (not Snoize — a live two-way exchange, not a passive capture) sent a Global Data Dump Request (Func=`0E`) addressed with the wrong channel byte, followed by a control request addressed with the correct one, with the device's Global MIDI Channel confirmed at 1 beforehand.

**Discovery:** the wrong-channel request (`F0 42 34 36 0E 00 F7`, channel 5, device actually on channel 1) produced **no response of any kind** — not a dump (Func=`51`), not a NAK (Func=`24`), nothing. The immediately following control request (`F0 42 30 36 0E 00 F7`, channel 1) produced a normal Func=`51` dump response right away, confirming the device, cabling, and script were all working correctly — the null result for the wrong-channel request wasn't a connectivity fluke.

**Consequence for the Global spec:** MIDI Global Channel — already known (Critical Discovery #83) to live in the SysEx header rather than the dump payload — is now confirmed to have **no safe write path via SysEx at all**. There's no dump field or Parameter Change to carry a new channel value, and now it's confirmed there's no way to provisionally address a channel the device hasn't adopted yet either — any attempt would simply be ignored. `X5DR_Global_Editor_Design_Spec.md` moves MIDI Global Channel to §6.1 ("no SysEx path exists") permanently, closing the last open item from Revision 3.

**Consequence beyond Global — a project-wide fact:** every SysEx exchange this entire app performs, across every editor (Program, Combi, Multi, Global, and any future Drums module), depends on the app's outgoing channel byte matching whatever the X5DR is actually configured to right now. If those ever disagree — a device reset to factory defaults on a different channel, a device shared with other gear on a non-default channel, a future multi-device feature — **the failure mode is total and silent**: no error, no NAK, no console warning, just nothing arriving back, indistinguishable from a disconnected cable or wrong port selection. This has been an implicit assumption of the whole app since Phase 1 (the established port/routing convention has always used channel 1) but was never confirmed as a hard requirement, nor surfaced anywhere as a risk, until this test.

**Verification:** hardware-confirmed via a live two-message exchange, both messages sent and both outcomes (one silence, one normal response) observed directly in the same test run — the strongest form of confirmation this project uses (compare to Critical Discovery #83, which was a passive capture requiring separate diff analysis; this was a direct behavioral test).

**Lesson:** this project's channel-addressing assumption (`g` = device's Global Channel) was documented from day one (`01_channel_messages.md`: *"g = Always Global Channel No."*) but its enforcement behavior — strict filter vs. informational — was never tested, because every prior session's hardware always happened to already be on the assumed channel. The gap was invisible until a test was specifically designed to probe it. Worth remembering for any future "the device isn't responding at all and I don't know why" debugging session — channel mismatch is now a confirmed, silent, total-failure candidate cause, not just Mode Change or port selection.

---

*Last updated: 2026-07-09 (Global Editor design session, Revision 4) — Critical Discovery #84 appended: a live addressing test confirms the X5DR's SysEx header channel byte is a strict filter — a wrong-channel Dump Request got zero response, while a same-second control request with the correct channel got a normal dump back. MIDI Global Channel is confirmed to have no safe SysEx write path and moves permanently to the Global spec's §6.1 "no path" list, closing Revision 3's last open item. This also surfaces a project-wide risk (new Landmine, Project Context): the entire app silently fails, with no error of any kind, if its assumed outgoing channel ever doesn't match the device's actual configured channel.*

## Critical Discovery #85 — Global's User Scale Grid Was Permanently Stuck Disabled on First Load, and the Gating Concept Itself Was Wrong

**Context:** Brief #23's implementation gated the 12-row User Scale grid's editability on `mainScaleType === 10` ("User Scale"), following the Global Editor Design Spec §2.2's instruction to use "the same enable/disable pattern as any other mode-gated control elsewhere in the app." The user then ran the full Brief #23 §4 hardware test pass and reported one exception: User Scale could not be edited at all — no increment/decrement, no direct input accepted — regardless of whether Main Scale Type was set to User Scale.

**Discovery 1 — the disabled state never updated after the panel's initial render.** `buildGlobalContent` computed `isUserScale = mainScaleType === 10` and set each row's `<input>.disabled` from it once, at render time. The Main Scale Type `<select>`'s `onChange` handler called `setParam('global.mainScaleType', v)` only — it never called `renderGlobalPanel()` or otherwise re-rendered anything, so the grid's `disabled` attribute never picked up the new value. Since the device's own default ships with Main Scale Type = Equal Temp (confirmed by Brief #23's baseline wire fixture, §2.1), every GLOBAL-tab-first-open rendered the grid disabled, and no subsequent dropdown selection — including selecting "User Scale" itself — ever re-enabled it, because nothing forced a re-render. Reproduced directly in the browser preview: injecting a fake snapshot with `mainScaleType: 0` and dispatching a `change` event on the `<select>` (value `10`) left all 12 `<input>` elements' `.disabled` unchanged (`true`) until a manual full-panel re-render was forced. Fixed by adding a `renderGlobalPanel()` call to the dropdown's `onChange`, the same convention already used elsewhere in this app for any control whose value gates other fields' enabled state (e.g. OSC Mode changes calling `renderProgPanel()`).

**Discovery 2 — the gating itself was the wrong design, not just unwired.** After the render-bug fix was verified, the user raised a design question: `GlobalSettings.userScale` (Design Spec §3.1) is a single, shared 12-note table — there are not two separate "Main User Scale" and "Sub User Scale" tables. It's addressable independently from either the Main Scale Type dropdown or the Sub Scale Type dropdown, and the two selectors are otherwise unrelated (Main Scale governs default note tuning; Sub Scale is selected in real time by an incoming MIDI CC#4 pedal switch per Design Spec §4.3). The device's own factory-default baseline capture (Brief #23 §2.1) demonstrates this concretely: Sub Scale Type = User Scale (`0x0A`) while Main Scale Type = Equal Temp (`0x00`) simultaneously — the exact combination the original gating logic would have made unreachable without a spurious, pointless round trip through Main Scale Type first. Gating User Scale edits behind Main Scale Type specifically was therefore not a hardware constraint at all, just an unexamined carry-over of "mode-gated control" phrasing from the Design Spec (§2.2) that didn't actually apply to a field addressable from two independent selectors. Fixed by removing the gating entirely — the 12 rows are now always editable, with no conditional title text, using the same plain `section()` helper every other Global section uses.

**Verification:** both fixes confirmed in the browser preview first (pure UI-state bugs, not wire-format bugs — no hardware needed to catch either one): (1) with a fake snapshot at `mainScaleType: 0`, dispatching a `change` event on the Main Scale Type `<select>` to value `10` flipped all 12 User Scale `<input>` elements from `disabled: true` to `disabled: false` immediately; (2) with the gating removed, all 12 rows rendered `disabled: false` regardless of `mainScaleType`'s value, and a direct-entry edit (`input.value = '42'`, dispatch `change`) committed to `store.getParam('global.userScale.0')` correctly. The user then re-ran the full Brief #23 §4 hardware test pass and confirmed User Scale editing now works correctly on real hardware, with no further exceptions reported — Global is fully hardware-verified.

**Lesson:** two independent lessons, one per discovery. (1) Any control whose value gates another control's `disabled`/enabled state must re-render (or otherwise explicitly propagate the new gating value) on every change — setting `disabled` once at render time is not self-updating. This exact shape (a value-gates-another-field's-editability control) is already handled correctly elsewhere in this app via inline sibling-toggle logic (e.g. the Pan "PRG" checkbox directly setting its neighboring numeric field's `.disabled` in its own `change` handler, Combi/Multi's timbre rows) — the Global bug was a case of a cross-render-cycle dependency (select in one section, grid in another) that the inline-sibling pattern doesn't cover, requiring a full re-render instead. (2) Language carried over from a design spec ("same enable/disable pattern as any other mode-gated control") should be checked against the actual data model before implementing, not applied by pattern-matching to surface-level phrasing — `userScale` was never actually "mode-gated" in the sense the phrase implied (owned by one mode, meaningless in another); it was a shared resource addressable from two unrelated selectors, and the device's own default configuration was direct proof of that the whole time, sitting in Brief #23's own wire fixtures.

## Critical Discovery #86 — Drum Kit Editing Has No Edit Buffer or Write Request; Same Persistence Shape as Multi Setup, Not Program/Combi

**Context:** design review of the existing DRUM EDITOR inner tab's placement inside Program Edit, prompted by a concern that a user editing a Program could reasonably assume Writing that Program also saves whatever Drum Kit it references.

**Discovery:** cross-referenced `02_sysex_format.md`'s full function code table and the Drums Data Dump (Func=`52`)/Drum Kit Parameter Change (Func=`53`) message definitions directly. Both are documented "R, T" with the identical phrasing already seen for Program/Combi's Edit-Buffer messages — but the destination differs: Func=`52` explicitly states *"Receives this message & data, save to Internal Memory"* — not an Edit Buffer — and no Drums Write Request function code exists anywhere in the table (unlike Program's `0x11` or Combi's `0x1A`). This is the identical shape Critical Discovery #60 already established for Multi Setup: the dump itself is the write, live and permanent, with no staging area and therefore nothing genuinely "abandonable" to track locally.

**Consequence for the design:** motivated abandoning the Drum Editor's placement inside Program Edit (which implies a save/discard lifecycle that doesn't exist for drum edits) in favor of a new standalone top-level DRUMS tab (Option B), rather than folding it into the newly-built GLOBAL tab (rejected — GLOBAL was deliberately built as a single flat, dump-only panel per Critical Discovery #81, and Drums' 2-kit × 60-slot live-per-note shape doesn't fit that without reintroducing the per-field-sync-mechanism complexity Global was built specifically to avoid). It also directly informed the decision *not* to force a Save/Discard gate on the PROG↔DRUMS nav-tab transition: Archive #20 already hardware-verified that the underlying Prog Edit↔Global Mode Change round trip is safe, since the existing (pre-relocation) inner-tab Drum Editor already performs this exact transition every time a user switches between DRUM EDITOR and any other Program Edit tab.

**Verification:** cross-checked against three independent pieces of `02_sysex_format.md` (the function code table, the Func=52 message definition, the Func=53 message definition), consistent with Critical Discovery #60's identical finding for Multi. The Mode-Change-round-trip safety claim reuses Archive #20's existing hardware verification directly rather than introducing new testing — the transition it depends on already runs continuously in shipped, hardware-verified code.

**Lesson:** the same lesson as Critical Discovery #81 (Global), now confirmed a second time for a different module — a missing Write Request function code in the table is itself a meaningful architectural signal, not a documentation gap to route around. Don't assume a module's persistence model from surface similarity to another module (Drums looks, superficially, like it belongs to Program because of where it currently lives in the UI); check the actual dump/write function codes directly.

## Critical Discovery #87 — `drums.*` Paths Pollute `dirtyParams`: Multi/Global's Already-Fixed Bug, Never Extended to Drums

**Context:** while designing how the PROG↔DRUMS nav-gate exception and dirty-scope banner should behave, read the local `setParam` wrapper and `getDirtyScope()` in the user-uploaded `index.html`/`store.js` to confirm current behavior before writing the Design Spec and briefs.

**Discovery:** `setParam` (`index.html`) has explicit `multi.`/`global.` branches routing those prefixes through `store.setParamQuiet` (Archive #73's fix) so they never enter the shared `dirtyParams` Set. **No equivalent `drums.` branch exists.** Every drum note edit — written via `getDrumStorePath(dumpIndex, field)` → `drums.${kitIdx}.notes.${noteIdx}.${field}`, called from the per-slot control handlers (`index.html`, lines in the 3660s–3740s at review time) — falls through to the wrapper's final, unguarded branch: `store.setParam(path, value); updateActionButtons(path.startsWith('combis.') ? 'combi' : 'prog')`. This marks the PROG action bar dirty/enabled from a drum edit alone, and adds the `drums.` path into `dirtyParams`. `getDirtyScope()` (which only recognizes `combis.N.`/`programs.N.` prefixes) cannot attribute it, returns `null`, and `showAbandonedModal` falls through to its Program-scope `else` branch — mislabeling the situation as an unsaved edit to whatever Program happens to be loaded.

**Verification:** confirmed via direct reading of both uploaded files this session — traced every call site writing a `drums.` path and confirmed all go through the local `setParam` wrapper (none bypass it via `store.setParam` directly), and confirmed `getDirtyScope()`'s exact two-prefix check against the current code. Not yet reproduced live in the browser this session (no code was changed) — the finding is a direct code read, same standard of evidence Critical Discovery #73 used for the identical Multi-side finding before its fix was implemented.

**Fix:** specified in Brief #24 — add a `drums.` branch to `setParam`, identical in shape to the existing `multi.`/`global.` branches, routing through `store.setParamQuiet`. Not yet implemented as of this write-up.

**Lesson:** identical to Critical Discovery #73's own lesson, now confirmed to have recurred: a dirty-scope exclusion fix established for one scope (Multi, then Global) does not automatically extend to a structurally identical later scope unless someone explicitly checks the wrapper's branches against every scope that should be excluded. Drums was never covered because it predates the entire dirty-scope architecture (Brief #16 onward) — it wasn't a regression, it was a gap nobody had reason to look at until this design review's persistence-model discussion (Critical Discovery #86) made the comparison to Multi/Global obvious.

## Critical Discovery #89 — Brief #25 Landed: Top-Level DRUMS Tab, Nav-Gate Exception, Dirty-Scope Banner, and One New Landmine-Grade Gap Found and Fixed Proactively

**Context:** implementing Brief #25 in full — relocating the DRUM EDITOR inner tab to a new top-level DRUMS tab, adding the standalone Kit 1/Kit 2 selector, wiring Mode Change entry/exit, the narrow PROG↔DRUMS nav-gate exception, and the generic "dirty scope elsewhere" banner.

**Implementation summary:**
- `buildDrumSlotData`/`renderUserKitPanel`/`getDrumStorePath` and all per-slot control wiring relocated as-is (a move, confirmed unmodified) from the retired DRUM EDITOR inner tab into a new `buildDrumsTabContent()`/`renderDrumsPanel()` pair, rendering into a new `#panel-drums` alongside a new `drums`-tagged top-level nav tab.
- ROM kits excluded entirely from the new tab per spec — the standalone Kit 1/Kit 2 selector (`drumsTabKitIdx`, new state) only ever addresses the two user-editable kits.
- Right column left present but empty (`.drums-xref-column`), reserved for Brief #26.
- New `editMode` value `'drumsTab'` introduced (Landmine #60), replacing the retired inner-tab's `'global'` value in the NAK-recovery mapping (`scope === 'drum'` branch).
- The nav-tab click handler's dirty gate now special-cases the PROG↔DRUMS edge (both directions) to call `navigateToDest()` directly, bypassing `store.isDirty()` entirely — the only such exemption besides the historical (now-removed) `dest === 'prog'` bypass this project deliberately walked back from (Landmine #32). Leaving DRUMS→PROG reuses the existing `switchToAndEditSlot` path already shared by combiEdit/multi/globalTab (added `editMode === 'drumsTab'` to that condition) rather than introducing a new navigation function.
- Extracted `dirtyScopeLabel(scope)` out of `showAbandonedModal` (previously inline) so the new `buildDirtyScopeBanner(onReturn)` component reuses the identical label-formatting path per Brief #25 §5 — not a second formatting implementation.

**New gap found and fixed proactively (not explicitly called out in the brief):** the BROWSER nav-toggle is reachable from any tab, including DRUMS, and is handled by its own click listener entirely separate from the nav-tab dirty gate (and therefore separate from the new PROG↔DRUMS exemption). `openPatchBrowser`'s `priorScopeType` ternary and `cancelPatchBrowser`'s scope branch — the exact mechanism Critical Discovery #79/Landmine #54 built for MULTI — had no `'drums'` case, so opening BROWSER from DRUMS and clicking Cancel would have silently fallen through to `'program'`, re-entering Prog Edit mode instead of restoring Global mode. Fixed by adding a `'drums'` case to both, identical in shape to the existing `'multi'`/`'global'` cases (mode restore only, no buffer resync, per Landmine #58). Landmine #54 amended to record this and to note GLOBAL's own equivalent case (added silently during Brief #23, never previously recorded here).

**Verification (browser, pre-hardware):** using a browser-injected `window.showOpenFilePicker` override (native file pickers aren't automatable in the sandboxed preview browser) to load the factory `.syx` reference file and select A19 `[ComboKit]` (a genuine Drums-mode program), confirmed all of the following directly in a live DOM:
- DRUMS tab renders: kit selector, relocated slot list + detail panel (identical fields/behavior to the old inner tab), reserved empty right column.
- Kit 1 → Kit 2 selector switch loads genuinely different slot data (confirmed distinct instrument names between kits).
- PROG (clean) → DRUMS: no banner.
- PROG (dirty, via a Level field edit) → DRUMS: no modal, banner renders with the correct label ("A19 [ComboKit] has unsaved edits."), dirty state untouched.
- Banner click-to-return (and the equivalent direct PROG-tab click): returns to PROG with the dirty edit (`Level = 50`) still intact, no modal.
- DRUMS → COMBI with the same dirty Program behind it: Abandoned Edits modal correctly fires, correctly labeled, "Stay" correctly cancels back to DRUMS.
- BROWSER opened from DRUMS, then Cancelled: status message confirms the new `'drums'` branch executed (mode-restore attempt reported, rather than silently behaving as if scope had been `'program'`).
- Program Edit's OSC tab confirmed to no longer show a DRUM EDITOR inner tab (the accepted interim state per Brief #25 §6, until Brief #26 adds the read-only summary).

Hardware verification (Mode Change wiring generating the correct wire bytes, ACK/NAK behavior, the Archive #20 mode-transition regression check in the new top-level-tab context) — per Brief #25 §8/§9 — was **not** performed this session; the sandboxed environment has no MIDI hardware attached. All 217 existing Vitest tests continued to pass; no new automated tests were added for the nav-gate exception or banner, since — consistent with Critical Discovery #88 — this logic lives entirely in `index.html`, which has no automated test harness by established project convention.

**Lesson:** the BROWSER-nav-toggle gap is the same shape as Critical Discovery #79's original MULTI finding, recurring a second time for a different scope — reinforces Landmine #54's own lesson that "no browsable list of its own" and "nothing to restore on Cancel" are two different properties, and every new scope-claiming tab needs both `openPatchBrowser`/`cancelPatchBrowser` cases checked explicitly, not assumed to follow from the nav-tab gate exception review alone (the two code paths are unrelated call sites over the same underlying state).

## Critical Discovery #90 — DRUMS→PROG Was Silently Discarding a Dirty Program's Edit Buffer on the Device (Editor and Device Diverged)

**Context:** the first hardware test of Brief #25 (flagged as outstanding in Critical Discovery #89). User's test: load a Program, edit a field (dirty), switch to DRUMS (device correctly enters Global mode), switch back to PROG (device correctly re-enters Prog Edit mode) — editor still shows the dirty edit, but the device's Prog Edit buffer had silently reverted to the clean, previously-saved patch. User separately confirmed that manually switching the device back to Prog Edit mode via the front panel (no software involved) preserves the dirty buffer correctly — isolating the cause to something the editor's software was sending, not an inherent device behavior.

**Root cause:** the DRUMS→PROG nav-tab branch (added by Brief #25) reused `switchToAndEditSlot(currentProgIndex)`, the same function already used for COMBI/MULTI/GLOBAL→PROG. That function's purpose is to guard against a manual front-panel program change made while the editor was on another tab: it exits to Program mode, resends Program Change to `currentProgIndex`, waits 100ms, then re-enters Prog Edit. The Program Change step is what silently discards the dirty state — sending Program Change to (re-)select a program, even the one already active, causes the device to reload that program from stored memory into its edit buffer, wiping any live-edited-but-not-written parameter changes.

This had never surfaced before Brief #25 because of an invariant the rest of the app enforces: the uniform `store.isDirty()` gate forces a Write/Discard/Stay decision before any nav-tab transition proceeds, so by the time `switchToAndEditSlot(currentProgIndex)` runs for COMBI/MULTI/GLOBAL→PROG, PROG itself is always already clean (only the *other* scope could have been dirty, and that was just resolved). Brief #25's PROG↔DRUMS nav-gate exception (Design Spec §6, Landmine #61) is deliberately exempt from that gate in both directions — specifically so a dirty Program's edits aren't disturbed by visiting DRUMS — which makes DRUMS→PROG the first-ever path where `dest === 'prog'` can run with PROG genuinely still dirty. `switchToAndEditSlot`'s Program Change resend was never designed against that case, because it never used to be reachable.

**Fix:** split DRUMS→PROG into its own branch, separate from the combiEdit/multi/globalTab branch, that sends only a bare Mode Change back to Prog Edit (`buildModeChange(MODE_PROG_EDIT)`) — no exit-to-Program-mode step, no Program Change, no re-entry delay. This exactly mirrors what the user's own front-panel test proved safe. No settling delay is needed since this runs from a synchronous nav-tab click, not an async continuation (Landmine #18/#41's distinction). DRUMS never changes which program is loaded, so there is no "manual front-panel program change" risk for this edge to guard against in the first place — the Program Change was pure liability here, not a safeguard.

**Verification:** browser-verified in this session (dirty edit survives the DRUMS→PROG round trip, no modal, no console errors); **subsequently confirmed on real hardware by the user** — the dirty Program's edit buffer is now correctly preserved across a PROG→DRUMS→PROG round trip. Closed.

**Lesson:** a function written to paper over one specific risk (a stale device selection from front-panel activity) can be actively harmful when reused in a new context where its own defensive action *is* the risk. The "only one scope can be dirty at a time" invariant this codebase has relied on since Brief #16 was true everywhere until Brief #25 deliberately broke it for one specific edge (by design, per the Design Spec) — and the code that assumed the invariant (`switchToAndEditSlot`) wasn't re-examined against the case the new exception introduced. Any future nav-gate exception that lets a dirty scope survive a tab transition must audit every downstream function the transition calls for hidden assumptions like this one, not just the gate logic itself.

---

Fixed by giving DRUMS→PROG its own branch (bare Mode Change only, no Program Change). One Decisions Made row appended. ## Critical Discovery #91 — Device Silently Reassigns a Drum Key Collision Instead of Rejecting It; Editor's Key Dropdown Didn't Account for This

**Context:** continued hardware testing of the relocated DRUMS tab (Brief #25). User attempted to reassign a slot's Key to a value already in use by another slot in the same kit.

**Discovery (user-reported, both directions confirmed):** the X5DR does not reject or NAK a Key assignment that collides with another already-assigned key. Instead it silently walks the keyboard in the direction of the requested move until it finds a free key, and assigns there instead:
- Example 1 (downward): keys D1 and D#1 already assigned to other slots. Reassigning a slot currently at E1 down to D1 results in the device actually assigning C#1 (continuing downward past both occupied keys until free).
- Example 2 (upward): keys D1 and D#1 already assigned. Reassigning a slot currently at B0 up to D1 results in the device assigning E1 (continuing upward past both occupied keys until free).

The editor's Key `<select>` (in `renderDrumDetail`) offered the full C0–G8 range (MIDI notes 12–115) unconditionally, with no awareness of what other slots in the same kit already used. Selecting a colliding key sent that raw value via `sendDrumParamChange`, and the editor's own `workingCopy` (and displayed Key field) recorded the requested key — not whatever key the device actually landed on. Editor and device silently diverged, with no error, ACK, or NAK to signal it — the same category of failure as Landmine #57 (silent channel-mismatch failures), just at the parameter-value level instead of the message-routing level.

**Fix:** added `getUsedKeysInKit(kitIdx, excludeNoteIdx)`, scanning the kit's 60 notes for enabled slots' keys (a disabled slot's stored key value doesn't sound and isn't a real collision). The Key `<select>`'s option-building loop (`index.html`, `renderDrumDetail`) now skips any key already used by another enabled slot, always keeping the currently-edited slot's own key visible regardless (even in the edge case where it coincidentally matches another slot's key due to a pre-existing data inconsistency). This was the user's own suggested fix, evaluated and adopted directly rather than attempting to model and replicate the device's directional collision-search behavior, which would need to exactly match undocumented device-internal search logic to stay correct — filtering to only-ever-valid options sidesteps needing to know the search direction at all.

**Verification:** browser-verified in this session (Key dropdown correctly excludes keys held by other enabled slots in the same kit — e.g. a 60-slot-enabled kit narrowed from 104 possible keys to 45), then **confirmed on real hardware by the user** alongside Critical Discovery #90 — the collision-reassignment behavior no longer occurs since the dropdown can't offer a colliding value in the first place. Closed.

**Lesson:** a device that resolves an invalid input by silently substituting a different valid one (rather than rejecting it) is a distinct failure mode from a NAK — there's no protocol-level signal to detect it by, so the only reliable fix is preventing the invalid input from being offered in the first place. Any other X5DR field with device-side collision-avoidance or similar silent-substitution behavior (none currently known) would need the same UI-level prevention, not a post-hoc detection mechanism, since nothing in the SysEx response distinguishes "accepted as sent" from "silently substituted."

---

## Critical Discovery #92 — Brief #26 Pre-Implementation Review Found Two Real Gaps and Confirmed a Layout Assumption Was Wrong

**Context:** reviewed `Brief-26-Drum-OSC-Summary-And-Cross-Reference.md` against the codebase as it stood after Briefs #24/#25, per the user's request to check for anything needing amendment before implementation.

**Finding 1 — field name.** The brief and Design Spec both refer to "the Program's own `osc.kit` field." No such field exists. Confirmed via `index.html`: the real field is `programs.N.osc1.multisound` (0/1 = User Kit 1/2, 8–15 = ROM Kit 1–8), used throughout the existing OSC-tab code (`buildOscContent`, `buildEasyOscPanel`).

**Finding 2 — Program No. resolution risk was misidentified; the real risk was absent from the brief entirely.** `encodeProgramNoParam`/`decodeProgramNoParam` (`midi/sysex.js`) are wire-layer helpers converting a live Parameter Change value to/from `{enabled, bankG, programNo}` — irrelevant to this feature, since `workingCopy` already stores `timbre.programNo`/`timbre.bankG` (Combi) and `track.programNo`/`track.bankG` (Multi) as plain decoded fields (confirmed via existing Combi/Multi Timbre/Track render code). No decode step is needed at all.

The actual risk: Landmine #50 (Bank G program data doesn't exist in `workingCopy`) applies directly here — naively indexing `workingCopy.programs[timbre.programNo]` without checking `bankG` first risks a false positive, since Bank G's `programNo` range (0–135) numerically overlaps Bank A's (0–99). The user then pointed out, and this was verified directly against the codebase, that the risk resolves cleanly: Bank G's own 8 drum-kit programs (**G129–G136**) are the ROM kits themselves — `BANK_G_NAMES[128..135]` is `'GM Kit', 'Power Kit', 'Analog Kit', 'Jazz Kit', 'Brush kit', 'Perc Kit', 'Dance Kit', 'Orch Kit'`, the identical 8 names (in the identical order) as `ROM_DRUM_KITS`. No Bank G program can reference a User Kit — a Bank-G-pointing Timbre/Track is a **guaranteed, definite non-match**, not an ambiguous "not checked" case. The `if (bankG) skip` guard is still required in the code (to prevent the index-collision false positive), but no special UI caveat wording is needed for Bank G specifically, simplifying the feature's scope language.

**Finding 3 — the 5×12 ROM-kit-reformat assumption is confirmed false with real data, and the user's stated preference reverses the brief's fallback plan.** The brief hedged: "if reformatting `renderRomKitList`'s output into 5×12 is awkward given its existing structure, flag this back rather than forcing a mismatched layout." Counting the actual `ROM_DRUM_KITS` array: 6 of 8 kits have exactly 60 entries, but **ROM Kit 6 (Perc Kit) has 78 and ROM Kit 8 (Orch Kit) has 61** — both exceed a fixed 60-cell (5×12) grid. Rather than falling back to ROM kits keeping their existing separate list-table format (the brief's implied fallback), the user explicitly preferred a single unified table format for both User and ROM kits for Phase 3 visual consistency, accepting variable row counts per kit, and requested the same column-major fill order (down column 1 first, then column 2, etc.) already used by `buildPatchTable`'s Patch Browser grids — rather than row-major.

**Resolution, implemented as Brief #26:** all three corrections applied (see Decisions Made rows above) — field name fixed; `getProgramsUsingKit`/`buildKitCrossReference` skip Bank G unconditionally with no special caveat; `buildKitSummaryTable` is one shared function for both kit types, reusing `buildPatchTable`'s exact `i = c * rows + r` column-major convention with `rows = Math.ceil(entries.length / 5)` computed per-kit.

**Verification:** browser-verified — OSC-tab Kit Summary confirmed correct for a User Kit (12 rows, matching the DRUMS tab's own slot order) and for ROM Perc Kit (16 rows, correct ROM data, confirmed the EASY tab has its own separate, non-rerendering duplicate Kit selector that must not be confused with the OSC tab's own — an existing `dataset.sync` lightweight-sync design, unrelated to this brief, that doesn't propagate to a full re-render). Cross-reference listing confirmed correct for two different User Kits on the same loaded Program set, each producing a distinct, plausible Programs/Combinations/Multi breakdown. All 224 Vitest tests pass (217 prior + 7 new, covering the resolution logic's positive case, negative/over-inclusion case, Bank G exclusion including the index-collision scenario specifically, and both `null`-category and `null`-array-entry handling). No hardware verification required or performed — both features are pure reads with no SysEx traffic, per the brief's own acceptance criteria.

**Lesson:** a design document's risk framing can point at the wrong function (the encode/decode helpers) while missing a real, already-documented risk (Landmine #50) elsewhere in the same feature — re-verifying against the actual codebase (not just the brief's own stated assumptions) before implementing surfaced both. Separately, a brief's own hedge ("flag it back if this doesn't fit") is only useful if someone actually runs the numbers against the real data before implementing, rather than assuming the common case (fixed 60-entry kits) generalizes — counting the real `ROM_DRUM_KITS` array took one command and changed the entire layout decision.

## Critical Discovery #93 — Code Audit Found the Current Stylesheet Has Zero CSS Custom Properties, No Orange Anywhere, and an Undocumented 8-Color Write-Button State System

**Context:** Phase 3 color-token planning session. After building a design taxonomy from Claude Design mockups (four mockups reviewed: Prog Mode Easy tab, Select Multisound browser, Unsaved Edits modal, VDF tab toolbar), performed the agreed Step 2 code audit — a full scan of `index.html`'s `<style>` block (1,252 lines, 292 color-bearing declarations) to catch anything the mockups hadn't shown, per the project's established "mockups won't cover 100% of the app" caution.

**Finding 1 — no theming infrastructure exists yet.** `grep` for `--[a-zA-Z-]*\s*:` (CSS custom property declarations) returned zero matches anywhere in the file. Every color is a literal hex/rgb/named value. This confirms Phase 3 is building the token layer from nothing, not retrofitting an existing one — relevant because it means there's no risk of a half-migrated intermediate state to reason about.

**Finding 2 — the current "accent" is blue, not orange, and is unrelated to the target M1-inspired palette.** `#2d68a2` (5 direct uses) plus three close variants (`#5b8dc4`, `#1a3a5c`, `#7ab8f5`) implement patch/browser selection highlight, active drum-kit toggle buttons, and a secondary `.toggle-btn` component. None of this survives Phase 3 — user confirmed nothing about the current blue is meant to persist as a second, distinct accent alongside the new orange.

**Finding 3 — an undocumented 5-state color system on the toolbar Write/Cancel buttons.** `.prog-actions`/`.combi-actions` (the "Write in place"/"Discard Edits" buttons, top-right of Program/Combi editors) implement: clean (`#6b6`/`#585`), dirty (`#cc8`/`#aa6`/`#2a2a1a` bg), failed (`#c55`/`#944`/`#2a1a1a` bg), success-flash (`#000` on `#33ff33`), plus a differently-colored cancel/discard state (`#b77`/`#855`) — 8 distinct hex values total, each with its own hover variant. None of this was visible in any mockup (the Claude Design mockups only showed a single static state of these buttons). This is a genuine gap the mockup-first approach alone would have missed entirely — confirming the value of doing the code audit as a mandatory second pass, not an optional one. Resolved by redesigning the whole system to reuse existing tokens (`--bg-button-neutral`, `--accent-line`, `--danger-border`, `--accent-fill`, `--danger-tint`) rather than tokenizing the 8 colors as-is — see Decisions Made table and `X5DR_Editor_Phase3_Color_Token_Spec.md` §5.

**Finding 4 — the "Unsaved Edits" modal currently has zero color differentiation.** `.modal-buttons button` (all three buttons: "Write to Device and Continue," "Discard Edits and Continue," "Cancel") share one plain gray treatment (`#333` bg, `#ccc` text) in the live code — the amber-tinted "Discard Edits" row from the Claude Design mockup doesn't exist in the app today at all. Worth recording so a future implementer doesn't go looking in the code for a value to "extract" — it needs to be built new, per the mockup.

**Finding 5 — an audit false positive, corrected within the same session.** The audit's first pass flagged `.prog-actions` and `.combi-actions` as "nearly verbatim" duplicated CSS and recommended deduping before the Step 4 tab-by-tab retrofit. A closer line-by-line diff (identical property values, differing only in the selector prefix) combined with re-reading a code comment directly above `.combi-actions` — which explicitly cites this project's ADR-0002 "duplication over abstraction" convention by name — showed the flag was wrong: this is deliberate, matching established project architecture, not an oversight. Recommendation retracted in the same session, before being acted on.

**Verification:** all findings confirmed via direct `grep`/`sed` inspection of the actual uploaded `index.html`, not inference from mockups or memory — hex value counts, selector contexts, and the ADR-0002 comment were all read directly from the file. No code was changed this session; this was a planning/audit-only pass. No Vitest run needed (no `.js` module touched).

**Lesson:** the two-pass approach (mockup-derived taxonomy, then a separate code audit) paid for itself directly — the write-button state system (Finding 3) would not have been discovered from mockups alone, since none of the four reviewed screenshots happened to show a dirty, failed, or success state. Separately, a comment explaining *why* a code pattern exists (here, an explicit ADR citation) should be checked before flagging that pattern as a defect — the first audit pass reasoned from the diff alone and missed a comment sitting three lines above it that answered the question directly.

## Critical Discovery #94 — Phase 3 Control Component Taxonomy Agreed; EG Curve Widget Behavior Corrected Against M1 Reference

**Context:** Phase 3 control-component design session, following the color token session (Critical Discovery #93). Performed a full code audit of the live `index.html` to inventory every current control (numCtrl, sliderCtrl, selCtrl, and bespoke builders like buildEgTimeMods, buildSinTriCtrl, buildTimbrePanCtrl), then resolved it into a small taxonomy.

**Finding 1 — most numeric fields have no slider at all today.** Only Effect params (ADR-0003) got the slider+field treatment; OSC level, VDA/VDF level, EG stage values, transpose/detune, Global tuning, and Drum tune/level/decay all use a bare number field. This is the bulk of what Phase 3's knob work replaces.

**Finding 2 — no dual-handle range slider exists.** Key Window Top/Bottom and Vel Window Top/Bottom are currently two independent, unlinked `numCtrl` fields with no cross-validation. Resolved as a new component (variant E), with handles clamped so they cannot cross — closest approach is both handles at the same value, retaining the editable numeric fields since overlapping handles are visually indistinguishable.

**Finding 3 — VDA EG stage levels are unsigned (0–99); VDF and Pitch EG stage levels are signed (−99…99).** Confirmed via direct comparison of `buildVdaSection` vs. `buildVdfSection`/`buildOscPitchEgPanel`. User confirmed intentional, not a latent bug — carries into the EG curve widget's two vertical-mapping modes (floor-referenced vs. center-referenced).

**Finding 4 — the EG curve widget's stage-transition behavior was initially mis-specified, corrected against a user-supplied Korg M1 VST screenshot (Prog Mode → VDA tab).** Initial design draft assumed a short stage flatlines at its terminal level for the remainder of a fixed per-stage pixel budget, then jumps to the next stage. The M1 reference shows this is wrong: a short stage transitions directly into the next stage's slope, right where it left off. The only flat segments are the Sustain plateau (fixed width, ~20% of total window) and the trailing line after Release completes. Corrected in `X5DR_Editor_Phase3_Control_Component_Spec.md` §2 before any mockup work began.

**Finding 5 — two inconsistent UI shapes existed for conceptually similar "value plus deliberate override" controls.** OSC Pan and Timbre/Track Pan use a mode-select-plus-hidden-field pattern; Drum Pan folds Off into a single flat option list. Resolved into one reusable component (knob + 0–2 direct-select override buttons for Off/PRG, icon-stacked beside the knob rather than a single cycling button, since these overrides are deliberate-but-infrequent choices that should stay one click away rather than requiring a click-through sequence). Applies to OSC Pan, Timbre/Track Pan, Timbre/Track Output Level's `127=PRG` sentinel, and Drum Pan.

**Verification:** design/planning only — no code changed, no hardware involved. Audit findings confirmed via direct `grep`/`view` of the actual `index.html` (10,540 lines), not inference from memory. EG widget correction confirmed via a genuine Korg M1 VST screenshot the user provided, not assumption.

**Lesson:** the same "verify against a real reference, not assumption" discipline that caught the write-button color system (Critical Discovery #93) applied here to interaction behavior instead of color — an EG curve widget spec drafted from first principles (proportional stretch-to-fill) matched neither the current code's own approach nor, more importantly, the real hardware-synth UI convention it's meant to visually match. A single screenshot resolved it in one exchange.
