## Critical Discovery #95 — Claude Design's Handoff README Misidentified the BROWSER Tab as Non-Existent; Corrected Against Live `index.html`

**Context:** Reviewing the Claude Design handoff package (a `README.md` plus a design-reference HTML file, produced by a Claude Design session working from the same `index.html`) for sufficiency before writing Brief 1. The README included a "known real-app tab set" note intended to prevent nav-related implementation mistakes: *"`PROG, COMBI, DRUMS, MULTI, GLOBAL` — five tabs... There is no separate top-level 'Browser' tab; sound browsing is a modal overlay."*

**Finding — this claim is factually wrong, confirmed by direct inspection, not by re-reading the README more carefully.** `index.html`'s nav markup contains six `nav-tab` elements, not five:
```html
<div class="nav-tab nav-toggle" data-tab="browser">BROWSER</div>
<div class="nav-tab active" data-tab="prog">PROG</div>
<div class="nav-tab" data-tab="combi">COMBI</div>
<div class="nav-tab" data-tab="drums">DRUMS</div>
<div class="nav-tab" data-tab="multi">MULTI</div>
<div class="nav-tab" data-tab="global">GLOBAL</div>
```
BROWSER sits in the same persistent top nav row as the other five, with its own dedicated CSS (`.nav-tab.nav-toggle`, `.nav-tab.nav-toggle.active`) — it is a real, styled top-level nav item. The user's own Korg M1 reference screenshot (shared earlier in this same Phase 3 effort) independently confirms the same layout convention: a BROWSER button in the top nav row alongside COMBI/MULTI/PROG/GLOBAL.

What *is* true, and is probably the source of the README's error: BROWSER behaves differently from the other five. It carries the `nav-toggle` class specifically so it can be excluded from the app's own persistent-tab-switching logic — `document.querySelectorAll('.nav-tab:not(.nav-toggle)')` appears at four separate call sites gating the logic that switches between persistent editor panes. BROWSER doesn't get its own persistent content pane; clicking it opens a modal instead. The README appears to have over-generalized "behaves differently, has no content pane of its own" into "isn't really a tab" — losing the fact that it's still a real, visually-identical-at-rest nav element that needs the same token-based color treatment as the other five, just with its own `.active`-state and toggle-specific styling carried forward distinctly.

**Verification:** confirmed via direct `grep` of the actual uploaded `index.html` for `data-tab=`, `.nav-toggle`, and the four `:not(.nav-toggle)` call sites — not inferred from the README's prose or from memory of the app's general shape. Corrected text was written and the user manually applied it to the README file used for the handoff.

**Lesson:** a second AI system reading the identical source file can still misdescribe it — this isn't a case where the two tools had different information, they had the exact same `index.html` and reached different conclusions. Any factual claim in a cross-tool handoff document that affects implementation scope (here, "how many nav tabs exist and what to build for each") is worth a direct grep-and-verify pass against the real file before it's trusted, even when the document appears otherwise polished and precise elsewhere in the same session.

## Critical Discovery #96 — Double-Click-to-Edit on a Draggable Control Needs Manual `pointerdown` Detection, Not Native `dblclick`, and Deferred (Not Synchronous) Focus

**Context:** Interactive review of Brief 1's knob components (variants A/B/C) asked for a specific interaction: a single click-and-drag anywhere on a knob's face — including directly over its centered numeric readout — must always turn the knob, while a double-click on the readout opens a type-to-edit input. The first implementation attempt used the native `dblclick` event on the readout element, with the readout's own `pointerdown` handler left un-stopped so a single-click-drag would still bubble to the knob's drag listener.

**Finding 1 — native `dblclick` never reliably fired.** Verified by direct testing in the browser pane, not by re-reading the code: dispatching a *synthetic* `dblclick` event via `element.dispatchEvent(new MouseEvent('dblclick'))` in a debugging session made the feature appear to work, because a synthetic dispatch invokes the listener directly regardless of whether a real double-click gesture would ever produce that event. Testing with an actual physical double-click (via the browser tool's `double_click` action, and independently via two closely-timed `pointerdown` events) showed the editor never opened. Root cause: the knob's own drag listener calls `e.preventDefault()` on every `pointerdown` (to suppress text selection while dragging) — in Chrome, this suppresses the native `click`/`dblclick` synthesis that would otherwise follow a `pointerdown`+`pointerup` pair on the same element, for that same interaction.

**Finding 2 — after switching to manual double-`pointerdown` detection (timestamp + position proximity), the editor still didn't stay open.** Instrumented logging showed the double-click *was* correctly detected, `startEdit()` *was* called, the `<input>` *was* created and received focus (`document.activeElement === input` confirmed true) — and then immediately blurred, reverting to the plain readout before any typing could happen. Root cause: `startEdit()` was being called *synchronously inside the qualifying `pointerdown` handler*, before the browser's own native mousedown/mouseup/focus management for that same physical click had finished running. Manipulating focus mid-flight like this races the browser's own default focus-handling for the same event, which then blurs the just-focused input right back out.

**Fix:** replace the `dblclick` listener with manual detection — track `lastDownTime`/`lastDownPos` on each `pointerdown`, treat a second `pointerdown` within 400ms and 6px of the first as a double-click, call `e.stopPropagation()` on the qualifying event only (so it doesn't also start a knob drag) — and defer the actual `startEdit()` call via `setTimeout(startEdit, 0)` rather than calling it inline, so it runs after the current click's native event/focus processing has fully completed.

**Verification:** confirmed via real interaction in the browser pane at every step — a physical `double_click` action via element ref (not a synthetic dispatched event), console instrumentation temporarily added to `controls.js` to trace the `pointerdown`→`startEdit`→`focus`→`blur` sequence, and removed once the fix was confirmed. Vitest tests updated to simulate two real `pointerdown` events at the same position (a `doubleClick()` test helper) rather than dispatching a synthetic `dblclick`, so the test suite actually exercises the real detection logic instead of trivially passing regardless of correctness.

**Lesson:** a synthetic `dispatchEvent()` call in a test or a debugging session proves a *listener* is wired correctly — it proves nothing about whether the *real browser gesture* that's supposed to trigger that listener actually will, especially once another handler on the same element chain calls `preventDefault()`. Any interaction verification claim ("double-click works") needs a real gesture, not a dispatched event standing in for one. Separately: any code that programmatically focuses an element as a *reaction to* a pointer/mouse event on that same element (or an ancestor) should defer past the current event's own native handling — synchronous focus-during-pointerdown/mousedown is a recurring trap, not specific to this one control.

## Critical Discovery #97 — Local Dev Server / Browser Pane Cache Can Silently Serve Stale JS Across Reloads, Even a Forced Navigate or a `git stash` Round-Trip

**Context:** While debugging Critical Discovery #96 and again while trying to A/B-compare Brief 1b's font swap against the pre-swap state, code edits made on disk did not appear to take effect in the browser pane after a page reload — including a `navigate` call with `force: true`.

**Finding 1 (during #96's debugging):** after removing temporary `console.log` debug statements from `controls.js` and reloading, the *old* debug log lines still appeared in the console. Direct `curl` against the dev server's URL, and a check of the file on disk (`grep -c DEBUG`), both confirmed the server was correctly returning the up-to-date, clean file content — the staleness was entirely on the browser side. `read_network_requests` showed the relevant JS module request returning `304 Not Modified` rather than a fresh `200`, meaning the browser was reusing a previously cached response body based on a conditional-request validator, without the debug-log-removal ever being reflected.

**Finding 2 (during Brief 1b's font A/B comparison):** after `git stash` reverted `index.html` on disk to the pre-font-swap state (confirmed via `grep -c loadTestData` on disk returning `0`), the already-open browser tab still logged output from a debug hook that only existed in the *stashed-away* (font-swap) version of the file — proving the same caching behavior survives not just a simple reload, but a full round-trip through unrelated git operations, as long as the same tab/session is reused.

**Fix/workaround:** opening a brand-new browser tab (`tabs_create` + `navigate`) reliably fetches current disk content (confirmed via `read_network_requests` showing a clean `200`, not `304`, and console output matching current disk state exactly). A direct `curl` against the dev server URL is a fast way to confirm server-side content independent of any browser caching layer, when in doubt.

**Verification:** cross-checked three independent ways for both incidents — direct `grep`/`curl` against the file/server, `read_network_requests` status codes, and console output — before concluding the staleness was a caching artifact rather than the code fix itself being wrong.

**Lesson:** when a code change doesn't appear to take effect after a reload — including a forced navigate — cache staleness must be ruled out (via a fresh tab or a direct `curl`) before concluding the fix itself is broken. This nearly produced a false negative during #96's debugging and would have produced a false "the font swap caused this" conclusion during the Brief 1b A/B comparison had the stale cache not been caught. Worth checking early in any "my fix doesn't seem to work" investigation in this project's dev setup specifically (Claude Browser pane + `npx serve`), not assumed to be a one-off.

## Critical Discovery #98 — Brief 1b's Apparent `.ctrl-row` Overflow at Narrow Viewports Was Pre-Existing, Not Caused by the Font Swap

**Context:** Brief 1b's mandated full-app visual pass (loaded via a temporary dev-only hook that parsed a real factory-sounds `.syx` dump, since no hardware or file-picker access was available) found several `.ctrl-row` instances — e.g. OSC tab's PITCH MG "Waveform" `<select>`, EFFECT tab's "Dry:FX Balance" slider+label — visually overlapping their neighboring column, at the ~650–800px viewport width the browser tooling defaulted to.

**Finding 1 — measured, not assumed, that the font swap was the cause.** Direct DOM measurement (`row.scrollWidth` vs. `row.clientWidth`) on the OSC tab's Waveform row showed a genuine ~60px overflow under Inter. Live-toggling `--font-ui`/`--font-mono` to plain `monospace` on `document.documentElement.style` and remeasuring the *identical* DOM elements (no reload, same data) showed ~58px overflow — a 2px difference, not the cause of a 60px overlap. The row's own math confirms why: `.ctrl-label` has a hardcoded `min-width: 14rem` (224px) that doesn't shrink, and `.ctrl-row select` has no width constraint at all — the combination already exceeds a ~275–301px column regardless of font.

**Finding 2 — the same rows render cleanly at the app's actual intended width.** Resizing the browser viewport to 1400×900 (a realistic desktop width) made every previously-overlapping row, and the Combi/Multi Zone tables, the Patch Browser modal, and the Select Multisound modal, render with no overflow or clipping at all. The app is Chrome/Edge desktop-only per project convention with no responsive/mobile design intent — the ~650–800px default viewport used by the verification tooling is simply narrower than the app has ever been designed or tested against.

**Verification:** the live token-swap A/B measurement (not a code revert, not inference) directly isolated the font variable as the only thing changing between the two measurements, on the same DOM, same data, same viewport — a stronger proof than comparing screenshots across separate page loads, which could confound font, cache staleness (Critical Discovery #97), or incidental data differences.

**Lesson:** an overlap found during a visual pass is not automatically caused by the change under test — the same "verify, don't assume" discipline applied elsewhere in this project (Critical Discovery #93's write-button color audit, #95's nav-tab count) applies to ruling a regression *out* just as much as confirming one *in*. A live A/B toggle on the actual suspect variable, remeasuring the same DOM, is a fast and conclusive way to settle it. Logged as a Known Outlier (pre-existing narrow-viewport layout fragility) rather than fixed, since Brief 1b's own scope explicitly excludes layout redesign.

## Critical Discovery #99 — Written Design Briefs Paraphrasing a Claude Design Mockup Are Not a Substitute for Checking the Mockup Itself

**Context:** Brief 2 (header/nav shell retrofit) was implemented from its own written text — "`.nav-tab.active` → `--text-primary` with `--accent-line` underline" — without re-opening the actual Claude Design canvas file (`X5DR Design Directions.dc.html`, turn 6a) that was already sitting in the repo. The real mockup shows solid pill-shaped tabs with sentence-case labels and no divider lines, not an underline. The same gap recurred independently for the Write/Discard action buttons (Brief 2b): the Color Token Spec's own §5 table describes the Dirty state as an outlined ghost-button, but the real mockup (confirmed against a user-supplied screenshot) shows a solid `--accent-fill` fill, visually identical to the Write-succeeded "Saved" state.

**Finding:** in both cases, the brief/spec document was written as a *summary* of the mockup — accurate on token/color mapping, but not independently re-verified against the mockup's own pixel-level shape/state details at implementation time. Neither error was caught by design review; both were caught only after the user visually compared the running app against the real design.

**Fix:** corrected both — nav-tab/header to pills/sentence-case/no-dividers (Brief 2 correction), and the Dirty Write button to a solid fill matching Saved (Brief 2b correction).

**Lesson:** a written brief is a *paraphrase*, not a substitute for the source artifact. When a Claude Design mockup exists for a UI element, re-check the actual mockup (screenshot or raw canvas HTML) at implementation time, not just the brief's own prose description of it — especially for shape, case, and state-color details, which are the parts most likely to get lost in summarization. Same "verify against a real reference, not assumption" discipline as Critical Discoveries #93/#95/#98, applied here to written specs rather than code.

## Critical Discovery #100 — Cross-Tab Parameter Sync (`syncByKey`) Assumed Every Synced Element Had a Native `.value` Setter

**Context:** found while planning Brief 3 (VDA tab rebuild), before any code was written. The Easy tab's own condensed VDA mini-section mirrors Level (via a bespoke OSC↔VDA sync block), Velocity Sense, and all 7 EG stage fields live, in both directions, via `panelEl.querySelectorAll('[data-sync="..."]')` + `subscribeTo` (`syncByKey`). That generic sync helper did `els.forEach(el => { el.value = v; })` — it assumed every synced element was a native form control with a real `.value` setter.

**Finding:** VDA's move to `knobUnidirectional`/`knobBidirectional`/custom EG-field components meant those elements became `<span>` containers exposing `_setValue(v)`, not a native `.value` property. `el.value = v` on such an element is a silent no-op — no error, no console warning, nothing visibly wrong until someone noticed the two tabs had drifted out of sync.

**Fix:** `syncByKey` (and the Level sync block) made polymorphic via a small shared `syncSetValue` helper — `el._setValue ? el._setValue(v) : (el.value = ...)`. Verified in both directions for Level, Velocity Sense, and an EG field before merging Brief 3.

**Lesson:** any future tab migrating from native-form-element controls to the Phase 3 component library must audit every cross-tab `data-sync` key it participates in — a generic sync helper written for the old control shape will silently stop working for the new one unless made shape-agnostic first. Not specific to VDA; any tab with cross-tab mirrors (check `syncByKey(...)` call sites) needs the same check before its own Phase 3 retrofit.

## Critical Discovery #101 — A Shared Pre-Phase-3 Helper Reused by a Not-Yet-Migrated Tab Must Not Be Modified In Place

**Context:** VDA's EG Time Vel/KBD Mod fields needed to move from a `<select>`-based control to a three-way toggle (variant D). The underlying helper, `buildEgTimeMods`, builds both the control and its byte-packing logic — and is also called by VDF's own EG Time Mod fields (`buildVdfSection`), not part of Brief 3's scope and still using the original `<select>`.

**Finding:** modifying `buildEgTimeMods` in place to swap in a toggle would have silently changed VDF's rendering too, with no test or review step positioned to catch it — VDF isn't part of Brief 3's diff or verification plan.

**Fix:** wrote a new, VDA-scoped `buildEgTimeModToggles` with the byte-packing math copied verbatim, leaving `buildEgTimeMods` and VDF untouched. Matches this project's established "duplicate across evolving tab families" convention (ADR-0002, also seen in `.prog-actions`/`.combi-actions`).

**Lesson:** before modifying any shared pre-Phase-3 helper as part of a single tab's retrofit, grep for every caller — if another not-yet-migrated tab depends on it, duplicate rather than parameterize, even for a small change. Generalizes Landmine #36's "check every helper's internal calls, not just its argument list" to the Phase 3 rollout specifically: a shared helper's *rendering*, not just its scope-sensitive internals, can leak across tabs at different migration stages.

## Critical Discovery #102 — A Hover-Revealed Child Hidden via `display:none` Shrinks Its Own Parent's Hoverable Area to Exclude It

**Context:** the universal readout stepper (hover-reveal up/down nudge buttons) worked passably for knob "beside" readouts but not for VDA's EG stage fields — hovering over an EG field's value didn't reveal the stepper until the mouse was precisely over the (very narrow) value text, and the stepper then appeared to its right, outside wherever the mouse already was.

**Finding:** the stepper's hidden state used `display:none`, removing it from layout entirely — contributing zero width to its container (`.ctrl-readout-wrap`). Unhovered, the wrap's own hoverable box was therefore only as wide as the value text itself; the stepper then rendered *outside* that box once revealed. Knob "beside" readouts happened to work anyway, by accident: their `.ctrl-knob-beside-text` ancestor is a flex column with the default `align-items: stretch`, which stretched the wrap to match the width of the label above it — giving far more margin than the wrap's own content required, masking the underlying problem.

**Verification:** `getBoundingClientRect()` on the stepper vs. its wrap, before any hover, confirmed the stepper's box extended past the wrap's own box under the old `display` toggle, and sat fully inside it after the fix — for both an EG field (no accidental stretch) and a knob readout (previously masked by the accident).

**Fix:** switched the injected stylesheet's hover-reveal rule from `display: none/flex` to `visibility: hidden/visible`, which reserves the stepper's layout space at all times. The wrap's hoverable box now always already includes the stepper, consistently, regardless of the caller's own layout.

**Lesson:** for any hover-reveal UI (not just this stepper — tooltips, inline action buttons, etc.), prefer `visibility` over `display` for the hidden state whenever the revealed element should live inside the same hover-trigger box as its always-visible sibling. `display: none` is only safe for hover-reveal when the trigger element's own hoverable area is independently guaranteed wide enough — fragile, and, as here, can depend on unrelated ancestor layout that has nothing to do with the reveal itself. Two smaller, related fixes landed alongside this one: the stepper originally used a plain `click` handler, which only fires on mouse-up, so the value changed once instead of continuously while held — fixed with a `pointerdown`-triggered press-and-hold repeat (immediate step, 400ms delay, then every 80ms, via pointer capture); and the browser's own native number-input spin buttons remained visible alongside the new themed stepper once a value was clicked into edit mode — hidden via the same injected stylesheet.

## Critical Discovery #103 — A Fixed-Pixel-Width SVG Control Needs Its Container to Be Responsive, Not Just Its Own Coordinate System

**Context:** `egCurveWidget`'s SVG uses a fixed logical coordinate system (`viewBox`) sized to the worst-case envelope width (every stage at max time) — a deliberate, already-correct design. But the widget's outer `<span>` wrapper was given a hardcoded pixel `width`/`height` matching that same worst-case size, with no responsiveness at all. On a narrowed browser window, the EG panel (which does scale, along with every other VDA panel) shrank around it, but the widget itself did not — overflowing its panel instead of shrinking to fit.

**Finding:** the widget's own drag-interaction math already read the SVG's live rendered size via `getBoundingClientRect()` at pointerdown time (Control Component Spec §5's own requirement, already followed) — so the fix only needed to touch the outer container's CSS, not any interaction code.

**Fix:** changed the wrapper to `width: 100%; max-width: <natural worst-case size>; aspect-ratio: <viewBox width>/<viewBox height>` — fills available width up to its natural size, never stretching beyond it, with height following automatically so the whole curve scales as one uniform, non-distorting unit as its panel narrows.

**Lesson:** a fixed internal coordinate system (viewBox, for scale-accuracy reasons) and a fixed *container* size are two separate decisions — the first should very often stay fixed (as here, to keep pixels-per-time-unit constant and readable), but the second should default to responsive (`width: 100%` + `max-width` cap + `aspect-ratio`) unless there's a specific reason it can't be. Any future control built on a similar fixed-viewBox/worst-case-size pattern should default to this responsive-container shape from the start rather than needing a hardware-review round-trip to add it.

## Critical Discovery #104 — Critical Discovery #103's Responsive Sizing Broke Cross-Element Alignment; Reverted to Fixed Dimensions Matched to Sibling Layout Tokens

**Context:** VDF hardware/visual review (Brief 4 follow-up) reported that the EG Intensity/Color Intensity knobs (VDF's hero column) and the Level panel (VDA) were misaligned against their adjacent EG panel — a fresh problem, not something either brief's own implementation-time verification had caught.

**Finding:** the misalignment was reproducible only at certain window widths, not others. Critical Discovery #103's fix — `width:100%` capped at `max-width`, with `aspect-ratio` deriving height from width — couples both dimensions of the widget to its container's width. As the browser window resized, *both* the widget's width and height scaled together, continuously, so any padding or height value tuned to align two elements at one window width silently drifted out of alignment at any other width. This wasn't caught during Brief 3 or the first pass of Brief 4 because both were verified at a single fixed browser-pane width, never re-checked after a resize.

**Fix:** removed the `aspect-ratio`/`max-width` responsive behavior from `egCurveWidget` entirely, for every caller (VDA, VDF, and the `?componentGallery=1` demo). The widget now takes explicit `width`/`height` config — both literal fixed pixel values, no percentage, no aspect-ratio — falling back to a fixed "natural" width computed from the stage geometry when `width` is omitted (still fixed, just not caller-specified). VDA and VDF now pass a `width` computed from the *same* CSS tokens (`EG_FIELD_COL_WIDTH_PX × 4 + EG_FIELD_GAP_PX × 3`) that size the 4 stage-field columns beneath the widget, guaranteeing equality by construction rather than by visual coincidence, plus a `height` tuned per tab to each one's specific alignment target (see the Decisions Made rows above and Critical Discovery #105).

**Verification:** `getBoundingClientRect()` comparisons of the aligned elements at four explicit browser-pane widths (1100px, 1300px, 1500px, 1900px) using real data loaded from the factory soundbank — confirmed pixel-identical alignment at every width, where previously the offset varied continuously with window width.

**Lesson:** this directly supersedes Critical Discovery #103's own stated lesson ("the [container] size should default to responsive... unless there's a specific reason it can't be") — needing a control's dimensions to exactly match a specific sibling element, not just "look reasonable in isolation," is such a reason. When two elements must align, deriving both from the same fixed, shared tokens is more robust than letting each scale independently via CSS percentages — even at the cost of shrink-to-fit behavior on narrow viewports. This project's Phase 3 tabs already assume a substantial minimum width (each column's own `min-width`, raised in the same session to 560px), so the tradeoff extends an already-accepted non-responsive-below-~1200px convention (Archive #98) rather than introducing a new one. Any future control needing to match a sibling's size should default to fixed-and-token-derived, not responsive, from the start.

## Critical Discovery #105 — Converting `min-width` to a Fixed `width` Silently Wrapped Labels, Reintroducing the Alignment Problem Being Fixed

**Context:** Critical Discovery #104's fix required `.vda-eg-field`/`.vdf-eg-field` (the small boxes showing each EG stage's numeric value) to have a genuinely fixed, known width — the widget's own new fixed `width` config is computed from it. The change was made by taking the existing `min-width: 4.8rem` and simply changing the property to `width: 4.8rem`, reusing the same number.

**Finding:** `4.8rem` had only ever been a *minimum* — a floor below which the box would look cramped, with room to grow if its label needed more space. As a fixed maximum, it was too narrow for the longest labels ("Release Time", "Release Level", and VDA's "Sustain Level"), which wrapped onto two lines. This inflated the field box's height, which inflated the whole fields-row's height, which inflated the EG panel's total height — silently re-breaking the exact alignment Critical Discovery #104's fix had just established, in a way that wasn't obvious from reading the CSS (nothing about `width: 4.8rem` looks wrong in isolation).

**Fix:** measured the true natural (unwrapped) width of every stage-field label by temporarily injecting a stylesheet (`white-space: nowrap` on the labels, `width: auto` on the boxes) and reading `getBoundingClientRect()` on each — found the actual maximum to be ~83.6px ("Release Time"/"Release Level"), not 4.8rem (76.8px). Set the fixed field width to `5.25rem` (84px, a small margin above the measured maximum) and recomputed every downstream constant derived from it: `EG_FIELD_COL_WIDTH_PX`, `EG_FOUR_COL_WIDTH` (the widget's own new fixed width from Critical Discovery #104), and `.vda-column`/`.vdf-column`'s `min-width` (raised 420px → 560px, since the fixed EG content is now wider and — unlike before, when everything scaled down together — no longer shrinks to fit a narrower column).

**Lesson:** a `min-width` value is not safe to reuse verbatim when converting a control to a fixed `width` — a minimum was only ever validated as "not too small," never as "sufficient for every case it constrains." Before fixing any dimension that used to be a minimum, measure the natural/unconstrained size of *everything* it bounds (every label in the set, not just the longest-looking one at a glance) rather than carrying the old number forward on the assumption that it was already correct.

## Critical Discovery #106 — Pitch EG's Decay Stage Targets the Centerline, Not Start Level — Correcting the Approved Mockup's Own Stated Design Intent

**Context:** Phase 3 Brief 5 (OSC tab rebuild)'s Claude Design handoff (`OSC_Design_Reference.html` + `OSC_Design_README.md`) described Pitch EG's Decay stage as ramping back to Start Level, "which doubles as the held sustain point until Release" — and the mockup's own demo data rendered exactly that way (Decay's end height matching Start Level's height).

**Finding:** this is wrong about the instrument's actual behavior, caught only because the user (with direct domain knowledge of the X5DR) corrected it during the brief-writing conversation, not by inspecting the mockup or inventory doc more carefully — neither would have surfaced it, since both consistently described the same (incorrect) behavior. Pitch EG is a pitch-offset envelope around the note's nominal/played pitch: Start Level and Release Level are transient "swoops" away from that pitch at note-on/note-off; Attack Level is the peak of the swoop-in. Decay always ramps back to the **centerline (level `0`, the note's actual sustained pitch)** — not to Start Level's value, which would make the note-on pitch offset permanent rather than transient.

**Fix:** `buildOscPitchEgPanel` (`src/index.html`) configures `egCurveWidget`'s `decay` stage with a hardcoded `level: 0, levelEditable: false` — not `level: startLevel`. `sustainAfter: 'decay'` inserts the held plateau at that same centerline height. `OSC_Design_README.md`'s "Pitch EG" note was corrected in place (not left to silently describe the wrong behavior for a future reader) rather than only fixing the implementation brief.

**Lesson:** a Claude Design mockup's own written intent (not just its rendered pixels — see Landmine #70's "mockup vs. paraphrase" pattern) can itself be wrong about domain/instrument behavior neither Claude Design nor a summarizing brief has independent means to verify. When a request explicitly invites correction ("push back if you foresee problems," "let me know if my understanding is incorrect"), a domain-knowledge claim about how the actual hardware behaves deserves the same scrutiny as a visual claim — verify against the person who knows the instrument, not just against the document that describes it.

## Critical Discovery #107 — Why OSC↔VDA Level Sync Is a Bespoke Block, Not a Plain `syncByKey`: Traced to a Phase 2 Parser Decision

**Context:** during Brief 5 review, it was asked why `osc{1,2}.level` and `vda{1,2}.level` need a dedicated, hand-written cross-tab sync block (`renderProgPanel`, `src/index.html`) instead of the generic single-store-path `syncByKey` every other cross-tab mirror uses.

**Finding:** traced to `src/midi/parser.js`'s Program dump parser (`decodeOscBlock`/`decodeVdaBlock`, both called from the same top-level parse function) — it reads the OSC Level dump byte once per oscillator and writes the same value into **two separate `workingCopy` locations**, `osc{1,2}.level` and `vda{1,2}.level`, rather than one canonical field both tabs' UI could read from directly. This is a Phase 2 data-model decision (Decision Archive, June 2026: "`osc1`/`osc2` as explicit named properties" — VDA and OSC were modeled as structurally separate objects before Phase 3 unified their rendering treatment), not something introduced by any Phase 3 brief. `syncByKey` only handles a single store path mirrored across multiple UI locations; here there are genuinely two paths that both need to end up numerically equal, hence the bespoke block's dual `subscribeTo` + cross-writing `setParam` shape.

**Not fixed:** collapsing this to one canonical store path (letting a plain `syncByKey` replace the bespoke block) is a legitimate simplification but would require changing the parser, the encoder, and already-hardware-verified VDA code (Brief 3) — real data-layer surgery, out of scope for a Phase 3 tab-rendering brief. Brief 5 preserves the bespoke block exactly, including its `data-sync="osc{1,2}-level"`/`"vda{1,2}-level"` keys on the new `knobUnidirectional` Level controls.

**Lesson:** when a cross-tab sync mechanism looks more complex than its neighbors, check whether the underlying store genuinely holds one value or two — a bespoke sync block is often evidence of a duplicated-at-parse-time data model, not an arbitrary implementation choice, and "simplify the sync" and "simplify the data model" are two different, independently-scoped changes.

## Critical Discovery #108 — Three Component-Library Extensions Needed for OSC's First-Time Variant Usage (Brief 5)

**Context:** OSC is the first tab to use `knobOffDetent` (variant C, Pan), `checkboxCtrl` (variant H, Key Sync), and a live-editable `egCurveWidget` start point (Pitch EG's Start Level) for real. All three components already existed in `src/ui/controls.js` (built in Brief 1 as dormant/demo-only, per Landmine convention) but had never been exercised against real field requirements.

**Findings, each requiring a small additive `controls.js` change:**
1. `knobOffDetent` had no `format` option, unlike `knobUnidirectional`/`knobBidirectional` — needed for Pan's device-accurate `A15…A1, CNT, B1…B15` readout (confirmed against the instrument, not the approved mockup's own decorative "L12"-style label, which turned out to be a red herring — see the Non-negotiable section of `X5DR_Editor_Phase3_Brief5_OSC_Tab.md`). Added `format` destructuring, forwarded to `buildReadout`, with an `offAwareFormat` wrapper so the `'Off'` string sentinel never reaches a caller's numeric format function.
2. `knobOffDetent`'s OFF-state rendering (opacity fade + cleared arc) had never been checked against a real mockup; the approved OSC mockup additionally shows a small always-present reference dot at the knob's floor/OFF-detent position, enlarged and accent-colored when actually off. Added both dots (`polarToXY` at `KNOB_SWEEP_START`) as a purely additive visual detail on top of the existing (confirmed-correct, user-reviewed) opacity dim — not a replacement for it.
3. `egCurveWidget` had no way to update `startLevel` after construction — every prior caller (VDA, VDF) hardcodes it to `0` with no live field. OSC's Pitch EG Start Level is the widget's first genuinely live, editable start point. Changed `startLevel` from a `const` destructure to a `let`, and added `windowEl._setStartLevel(v)`, mirroring the existing `_setStages`/`_getStages` pair.

**Lesson:** "dormant since Brief 1, demo-only" components should be expected to need small, additive extensions the first time a real tab's actual field requirements exercise them fully — matches the exact same pattern Brief 4 hit with `toggleButtonGroup`'s icon-item extension (Critical Discovery, Brief 4 §5). None of these three changes altered any existing call site's behavior (all existing tests/usages pass `format`/omit the new dot/never call `_setStartLevel`, so nothing changes for them) — check that a new variant's first real use doesn't require anything beyond additive, backward-compatible config before assuming the dormant implementation is already complete.
